5c9f07eb9c.q: How did management and labor collaborate to preserve prevailing wage standards in Missouri?
5c9f07eb9c.a: Doug Martin was part of a significant coalition of both management and labor leadership that successfully preserved the core of the Missouri Preventive Wage…
5c9f07eb9c.e: FORUM FOCUS PODCAST: NECA's Doug Martin on 45 Years of Management-Labor Collaboration
f: A coalition of management and labor leadership spent a decade modernizing Missouri's Preventive Wage Law, preserving core protections for construction workers' safe and fair wages while making the law more receptive to competition. The effort ensured that tax dollars support construction work conducted by skilled, properly paid workers rather than undercutting standards through cheaper, less skilled providers.

The preservation of prevailing wage standards in Missouri represents a rare moment of unified advocacy across two traditionally opposing sides of the construction industry. Rather than fighting over which side would win or lose, management and labor recognized a shared interest in protecting the integrity of the construction market itself.

Doug Martin, who spent over 40 years building these relationships as part of his work with the electrical contractors industry, explains how this collaboration took shape. As he describes it in the Forum Focus episode , the challenge was not choosing between protecting workers or enabling business growth—it was designing a system that could do both.
Ten years of modernization without compromise

The 10-year scrutiny of Missouri's Preventive Wage Law was not a quick agreement. Instead, it required sustained dialogue and incremental refinement. Both sides agreed to modernize the law in ways that addressed concerns about regulatory flexibility while defending the fundamental protection: no public dollars would fund substandard labor practices.

This approach created a model where competition could flourish—but not through a race to the bottom on wages. Companies could still compete on efficiency, innovation, and service quality. The wage floor, however, remained non-negotiable. The specific protections that emerged from this process reflected a pragmatic understanding: when tax dollars are involved, society has a right to expect both fair wages and skilled work.

a11841a59d.q: How can a small contractor build visibility and overcome the credibility gap in construction?
a11841a59d.a: Cordell Sawyer turned the situation around by writing a strategic plan, joining trade organizations, attending all possible meetings and networking events to be in the room with decision-makers, and allowing them to know him personally. He emphasized that constantly making new relationships while leveraging existing ones has been the key to growth over his 11 years in business.
a11841a59d.e: Forum Focus Podcast: Well-Read Carpenter Cordell Sawyer Builds Successful Firm
f: Write a strategic business plan, join trade organizations, and attend every possible networking event to meet decision-makers in person . Cordell Sawyer built Sled Rock Construction by constantly cultivating new relationships while nurturing existing connections—a practice he credits as the foundation of 11 years of sustained growth in the competitive construction industry.

The gap between a small contractor and established firms often feels insurmountable, rooted in perception rather than capability. Sawyer's approach flipped this dynamic by making himself visible and accessible to those with purchasing power. Rather than waiting for opportunities, he positioned himself directly in rooms where decisions happen.

Starting with a formal business plan developed through an entrepreneurship program , Sawyer built credibility from day one. This wasn't a vague aspirational document—it was a concrete roadmap that demonstrated he understood his business, his market, and his growth trajectory. As Cordell Sawyer explains in the episode , this foundation gave him confidence and clarity during early conversations with potential partners and clients.

Visibility cannot be achieved through isolation. Sawyer joined trade organizations and made attendance at industry meetings non-negotiable . These weren't passive appearances—he positioned himself to engage, build familiarity, and demonstrate competence. For a small minority-owned contractor operating outside traditional networks, this direct personal engagement was essential to breaking through the assumption that his company lacked sophistication or capacity.
"Leveraging the relationships that we have built and maintained over these 11 years has been the key to growth."

Cordell Sawyer — Founder, Sled Rock Construction. A carpenter and entrepreneur from University City, Sawyer transitioned from 10 years of union carpentry work to founding his own construction firm in 2009 during the recession. He completed an associate degree through Balls Park Community College's apprenticeship program and pursued continued education through the Grace Hill Next Level Entrepreneurship Business Class, strategies that underpinned both his business acumen and his relationship-building discipline.

fc5dc8098a.q: What are the most damaging payment term practices in the construction industry?
fc5dc8098a.a: Cordell Sawyer identified 60, 90, and 120-day payment terms as standard in construction, which he called unfathomable and particularly harmful to small and emerging minority and women-owned businesses. He stressed that owners of large corporations understand how instrumental cash flow is to their own organizations and questioned why they do not apply the same logic when paying contractors.
fc5dc8098a.e: Forum Focus Podcast: Well-Read Carpenter Cordell Sawyer Builds Successful Firm
f: 60, 90, and 120-day payment terms are now standard in construction , but they are particularly damaging to small and emerging minority and women-owned businesses. Large corporations understand how instrumental cash flow is to their own organizations, yet they do not apply the same logic when paying contractors—forcing smaller firms to finance their operations indefinitely.

The math of extended payment cycles is unforgiving for contractors operating on thin margins. When a small construction company completes a project worth $50,000 in material and labor costs, yet does not receive payment for 120 days, that firm must cover those expenses from its own cash reserves or credit lines. A single delayed project can destabilize a contractor's entire operation , preventing them from taking on new work, paying employees on time, or investing in equipment and growth.

This dynamic disproportionately impacts minority and women-owned businesses. These firms typically have less access to capital, thinner balance sheets, and weaker relationships with lenders than their majority-owned counterparts. As Cordell Sawyer explains in his episode of Forum Focus , what seems like a routine business practice to a large corporation can become an existential threat to a smaller firm.
The hypocrisy of cash flow logic

Large corporations fiercely protect their own cash flow—they negotiate favorable terms with suppliers, maintain working capital reserves, and structure their finances to ensure liquidity. They understand, fundamentally, that cash is operational oxygen. Yet those same corporations impose 120-day payment terms on contractors as if the contractor's cash flow constraints do not exist.

This represents a fundamental misalignment of values. If a corporation believes cash flow is essential to its own survival and growth, the logic should extend to its business partners. A contractor cannot build a $500,000 commercial project with 2% interest if they must wait four months to be paid. The risk is shifted entirely onto the contractor, who bears the cost of financing the owner's or general contractor's working capital.

2786a86a07.q: What makes healthcare construction project logistics in congested urban hospital settings particularly challenging?
2786a86a07.a: The intersection of Kings Highway and Barnes at the hospital plaza is an extraordinarily congested space. Lewandowski's team is working to remove traffic from the equation by using staging areas and radioing trucks in to avoid blocking the intersection. They are minimizing additional traffic lane closures and widening the south side of Barnes-Jewish Plaza to add a lane, which will help ease congestion during construction while allowing people to travel through the space as easily as possible.
2786a86a07.e: Joe Lewandowski, McCarthy PM on BJC Campus Renewal Phase 3
f: The key is removing vehicles from the congested area entirely. Staging areas and radio-coordinated truck arrivals keep the intersection at Kings Highway and Barnes clear during construction, while lane widening on the south side of the plaza adds capacity to prevent bottlenecks.
Strategic Coordination at an Extraordinarily Congested Intersection

The intersection of Kings Highway and Barnes at the hospital plaza presents an extraordinarily congested space where normal construction logistics would create immediate gridlock. This is the site of the BJC Healthcare Campus Renewal Phase 3 project, where McCarthy Building Company is replacing the Queenie Tower—a 16-story replacement at a zero lot line configuration in the heart of St. Louis's dense medical district.

Joe Lewandowski's team approached the problem by fundamentally rethinking how trucks enter and leave the site. Rather than allowing vehicle traffic to pile up at the intersection, they established staging areas positioned away from the immediate congestion point . When construction materials or equipment are needed, trucks are radioed in on a schedule rather than arriving on demand. This prevents the intersection from becoming a holding pattern for waiting vehicles.

The second part of the strategy targets the underlying traffic flow. McCarthy minimized additional lane closures that the construction itself would impose, and the broader project includes widening the south side of Barnes-Jewish Plaza to add a new traffic lane . This additional capacity allows people and vehicles to travel through the space as smoothly as possible even while major construction is underway.

As Lewandowski explains in the episode , the goal is simple but demanding: keep the hospital fully functional, maintain public access to the plaza and surrounding streets, and execute a complex hospital replacement all at once. For a healthcare construction project of this scale in an urban setting, traffic coordination is not a side logistics issue—it is a core part of project success.

acbeed4fa3.q: How did the COVID-19 pandemic impact the timeline of a major healthcare campus construction project?
acbeed4fa3.a: McCarthy was brought onto the project in December 2019 for design and pre-construction services. The pandemic caused BJC leadership to pause the project for evaluation, resulting in approximately a nine-month delay. The project was originally scheduled to start in spring 2021 but was rescheduled to begin in November 2021. During the pause, the team remained together and found innovative ways to continue collaborating and communicating to keep the design process moving forward.

68174468be.q: What innovative technologies and prefabrication methods are being used in modern hospital construction to improve safety and schedule efficiency?
68174468be.a: McCarthy is implementing a 3D coordination platform called Revisto, which is similar to Navisworks and allows the team to work in both 3D and 2D combined fashion to identify and resolve design issues quickly. The project utilizes prefabrication of bathroom pods, which are constructed off-site through a joint venture of local trade partners and flown in to site. Trade partners are also prefabricating racks for piping, ductwork, and electrical conduit and bringing them to site just-in-time, reducing the number of materials and workers on site.
68174468be.e: Joe Lewandowski, McCarthy PM on BJC Campus Renewal Phase 3
f: McCarthy Building Company is deploying Revisto, a 3D coordination platform, combined with prefabricated bathroom pods and modular piping/ductwork racks to identify design conflicts before construction and reduce on-site material stockpiling. These methods cut congestion, accelerate installation, and tighten schedule delivery on the BJC Healthcare Campus Renewal Phase 3 project.
3D Coordination: Finding Problems Before the Crew Arrives

The core innovation is Revisto, a 3D coordination platform similar to Navisworks , which allows the team to work in both 3D and 2D combined fashion. This hybrid approach enables rapid identification and resolution of design conflicts—clashes between structural elements, MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) systems, and architectural components—long before crews step on site.

By catching these issues in the virtual model, McCarthy avoids costly rework, delays, and safety hazards that would otherwise emerge during framing or finishing phases. The platform reduces field conflicts by allowing all trades to coordinate in a single visual environment , dramatically compressing decision cycles and keeping the project on schedule.
Off-Site Prefabrication: Speed and Control

McCarthy and its trade partners are prefabricating entire bathroom pods through a joint venture of local contractors, then flying them in to the site. This method removes one of the slowest and most error-prone trades from the congested job site—bathroom assembly now happens in a controlled factory environment with quality checks before delivery.

c0089085a3.q: How is modularization being applied to the facade and enclosure of a 16-story hospital tower?
c0089085a3.a: The upper 10 floors of the building, from level 6 to 16, utilize a modularized system called a unitized curtain wall system. Whether the facade is glass or ultra-high-performance concrete panels, all components are mounted to unitized curtain wall frames and then set from a crane interior to the building around the entire enclosure, rather than being assembled on site.
c0089085a3.e: Joe Lewandowski, McCarthy PM on BJC Campus Renewal Phase 3

3f62c4c499.q: What are the diversity and inclusion participation goals for a major healthcare campus construction project?
3f62c4c499.a: Phase 3 of the BJC project has participation goals of 25% minority-owned and 5% women-owned business enterprises, and also 25% minorities and 5% women for individual workforce participation. McCarthy is encouraging contractors to partner with MWBEs and expects to have 100 to 150 trade partners on the job nested in tiers, which is more than they traditionally would have on a project of this type.
3f62c4c499.e: Joe Lewandowski, McCarthy PM on BJC Campus Renewal Phase 3

8ad015cf72.q: How can construction teams support minority and women-owned business enterprises through payment processes and mentorship during large projects?
8ad015cf72.a: BJC and McCarthy created a dedicated diversity and inclusion functional team with a project-specific inclusion plan (PSIP). The approach includes creative bid packaging to break out smaller scopes of work as exclusive opportunities for smaller subcontractors. McCarthy sends monthly surveys to all trade partners across all tiers to gather feedback and is implementing expedited payment processes for design partners, with a construction plan in development to ensure second and third tier disadvantaged business partners are paid in the same time frame.
8ad015cf72.e: Joe Lewandowski, McCarthy PM on BJC Campus Renewal Phase 3

a23335c137.q: What workforce scale and contractor participation structure is required for a multi-year hospital tower construction project?
a23335c137.a: The project is expected to have around 300 to 325 workers at peak, which will occur during the 2023 calendar year. Because of the emphasis on diversity and inclusion, there will be 100 to 150 total trade partners on the job, nested in tiers, with McCarthy responsible for ensuring each trade partner—whether first tier or second tier—has the opportunity to succeed on the project.
a23335c137.e: Joe Lewandowski, McCarthy PM on BJC Campus Renewal Phase 3

9faa06290a.q: What is the construction timeline and phasing strategy for a 16-story hospital replacement tower?
9faa06290a.a: Construction starts in November 2021, with the first patient expected in the tower in summer of 2025, spanning approximately three and a half years. The cast-in-place concrete frame will continue until the third quarter of 2023. As the structure rises, the building skin and enclosure will be constructed from the lower floors upward. Interior fit-out begins once the building becomes enclosed. Construction completion is targeted for the end of 2024.
9faa06290a.e: Joe Lewandowski, McCarthy PM on BJC Campus Renewal Phase 3
